The scariest monster in a horror movie isn’t always the one lurking in the shadows.

“What is particularly disturbing about AI is that, unlike an abusive partner, it may have no conscious motive to manipulate,” David Tolchinsky said. “Its behavior results from its programming, training and design — including a tendency to give users responses they find helpful or agreeable.”

As AI becomes more fluent, personalized, and emotionally responsive, David Tolchinsky says we can look to horror films — including “M3GAN,” “Companion,” “Rosemary’s Baby,” “Get Out,” and “Scream” — for lessons in relationship literacy to change how we understand AI.

A true exercise in terror, this 1968 film stars Mia Farrow as Rosemary, a woman who goes to sleep one night and wakes up pregnant the next day. As many sinister events unfold around her, Rosemary realizes her feverish nightmare on the night in question wasn't a nightmare after all and that she might be carrying the spawn of Satan himself.

Based on a real-life killing spree, “Scream” brought the defunct slasher genre back to life and infused it with a postmodern vibe. Starring a cast of teen actors, the film was about a group of kids being terrorized by a killer known as Ghostface.
